{{short description|Measure of distance between two proportions}}
{{DISPLAYTITLE:Cohen's ''h''}}
In [[statistics]], '''Cohen's ''h''''', popularized by [[Jacob Cohen (statistician)|Jacob Cohen]], is a measure of distance between two proportions or [[probability|probabilities]]. Cohen's ''h'' has several related uses:
* It can be used to describe the difference between two proportions as "small", "medium", or "large".
* It can be used to determine if the difference between two proportions is "[[clinical significance|meaningful]]".
* It can be used in calculating the [[sample size determination|sample size]] for a future study.

When measuring differences between proportions, Cohen's ''h'' can be used in conjunction with [[statistical hypothesis testing|hypothesis testing]]. A "[[statistical significance|statistically significant]]" difference between two proportions is understood to mean that, given the data, it is likely that there is a difference in the population proportions. However, this difference might be too small to be meaningful—the statistically significant result does not tell us the size of the difference. Cohen's ''h'', on the other hand, quantifies the size of the difference, allowing us to decide if the difference is meaningful.

== Uses ==
Researchers have used Cohen's ''h'' as follows.
* Describe the differences in proportions using the [[rule of thumb]] criteria set out by Cohen.<ref name="Cohen 1988">{{cite book | title=Statistical Power Analysis for the Behavioral Sciences | author=Cohen, Jacob | year=1988 | edition=2nd}}</ref> Namely, ''h'' = 0.2 is a "small" difference, ''h'' = 0.5 is a "medium" difference, and ''h'' = 0.8 is a "large" difference.<ref>{{cite journal | title=The Patient Health Questionnaire-9 for measuring depressive symptoms among the general population in Hong Kong | author=Yu, Xiaonan | journal=Comprehensive Psychiatry | year=2012 | volume=53 | issue=1 | pages=95–102 | doi=10.1016/j.comppsych.2010.11.002 | pmid=21193179 | display-authors=etal}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal | title=Characteristics of Youths With Hearing Loss Admitted to Substance Abuse Treatment | author=Titus, Janet C. | journal=Journal of Deaf Studies and Deaf Education |date=February 2008  | doi=10.1093/deafed/enm068 | display-authors=etal | volume=13 | issue=3 | pages=336–350| pmid=18252698 | doi-access= }}</ref>
* Only discuss differences that have ''h'' greater than some threshold value, such as 0.2.<ref name="Reavley">{{cite journal | title=Stigmatising attitudes towards people with mental disorders: Changes in Australia over 8 years | author=Reavley, Nicola J. | journal=Psychiatry Research | year=2012 | volume=197 | issue=3 | pages=302–306 | doi=10.1016/j.psychres.2012.01.011 | pmid=22417929 | s2cid=33538798 | display-authors=etal}}</ref>
* When the sample size is so large that many differences are likely to be statistically significant, Cohen's ''h'' identifies "meaningful", "[[clinical significance|clinically meaningful]]", or "practically significant" differences.<ref name="Reavley"/><ref>{{cite journal | title=Intentions and helpfulness beliefs about first aid responses for young people with mental disorders: Findings from two Australian national surveys of youth | author=Yap, Marie Bee Hui | journal=Journal of Affective Disorders | year=2012 | volume=136 | issue=3 | pages=430–442 | doi=10.1016/j.jad.2011.11.006 | display-authors=etal | pmid=22137764}}</ref>

== Calculation ==
{{Further|Binomial proportion confidence interval}}

Given a probability or proportion ''p'', between 0 and 1, its [[arcsine transformation]] is

: <math>\varphi = 2 \arcsin \sqrt{p}.</math>

Given two proportions, <math>p_1</math> and <math>p_2</math>, ''h'' is defined as the difference between their arcsine transformations.<ref name="Cohen 1988"/> Namely,

: <math>h = \varphi_1 - \varphi_2.</math>

This is also sometimes called "directional ''h''" because, in addition to showing the magnitude of the difference, it shows which of the two proportions is greater.

Often, researchers mean "nondirectional ''h''", which is just the absolute value of the directional ''h'':

: <math>h = \left| \varphi_1 - \varphi_2 \right|.</math>

In [[R (programming language)|R]], Cohen's ''h'' can be calculated using the <code>ES.h</code> function in the <code>pwr</code> package<ref>{{cite web | url=https://cran.r-project.org/package=pwr | title=pwr: Basic Functions for Power Analysis | date=2015 | author=Champely, Stephane}}</ref> or the <code>cohenH</code> function in the <code>rcompanion</code> package.<ref>{{cite web | url=https://cran.r-project.org/package=rcompanion | title=rcompanion: Functions to Support Extension Education Program Evaluation | date=2020 | author=Mangiafico, Salvatore}}</ref>

== Interpretation ==
Cohen<ref name="Cohen 1988"/> provides the following descriptive interpretations of ''h'' as a [[rule of thumb]]:
* ''h'' = 0.20: "small effect size".
* ''h'' = 0.50: "medium effect size".
* ''h'' = 0.80: "large effect size".

Cohen cautions that:
{{quote|As before, the reader is counseled to avoid the use of these conventions, if he can, in favor of exact values provided by theory or experience in the specific area in which he is working.}}

Nevertheless, many researchers do use these conventions as given.
